name: Freya Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. I'll keep this confidential. Tell me about yesterday at work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I spent the morning at Marsh & Finch trying to match a small theatre's ticket sales with the bank deposits, then I phoned them about a stack of unclaimed invoices. I'm 43, an experienced mid-level accountant, about average at the job; I have a bachelor's degree and a professional accountancy qualification. I enjoy making a confusing account legible for a volunteer treasurer, and I dislike the moment a late file means staying after the school bell.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the rest of the day look like at home, and where does AI enter?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Owen works as a groundskeeper, and our children, aged seven and eleven, take turns forgetting their lunch boxes. We have a mortgage, my accountant pay is low for the role, less than a month of expenses saved and few similar firms nearby. I use AI every day to group ticket receipts and draft questions, then compare the totals with the bank statement. I will try a new tool early, but I believe the staff and clients deserve a voice about how their records are used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a faster ticket sort helps if a human can still tell the theatre why the bank total differs. I'd ask the partners to show any new target to the staff before changing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages cover the mortgage when Owen gets full groundskeeping hours, but the savings would not cover even one whole month. My job probably stays in a plateau, yet a rainy month with fewer outdoor shifts already makes the kitchen budget tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the AI receipt grouping I already use and check the bank total myself. In the first year we'd put twenty-five a week into a bills account by cancelling the extra streaming package, as long as both wages arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about money even when the tool changes little. A wet month can already make the loan feel too large.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens on a rainy week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen may lose a day of grounds work, and we make a smaller food order. I try not to let the children notice, but the cupboard does look different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which number would you refuse to trust from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ticket refund total, because a show cancelled late can move payments across two bank dates. I check the original sales report before telling a volunteer treasurer what they owe.

I would ask staff to see any **new target** first.
think: My **job probably stays**, but we have less than a month saved.
Owen’s **weather-dependent hours** already strain our mortgage budget.
do: Keep checking **ticket refunds** against bank dates after daily AI grouping.
Save **twenty-five weekly** by cancelling one streaming package while both wages arrive.
feel: She feels **anxious** because ordinary lost shifts threaten the household budget.

steps.text: Keep checking ticket refunds against bank dates after daily AI grouping
Save twenty-five weekly by cancelling extra streaming package while both wages arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that the firm should show us the error rate before it raises our daily targets. If AI writes the first client email, someone should still be paid to read it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm to cut at least one paid day from my checking and client replies once the new software handles them. I'm not the top accountant here, and with less than a month saved I could not absorb much of a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose a paid two-week trial on closed theatre accounts, with the senior checking the AI's refund totals, and bring the results to the staff meeting. In the first year of steady change, if my paid days drop below four, I'd apply for posted finance-assistant jobs at the local arts centre while keeping funded work at Marsh & Finch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I could lose enough hours to miss a mortgage payment. A clever trial only helps if the job survives it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partners refuse a paid trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the approved grouping tool and the bank check I know, then ask the staff representative to record the refusal. I would not test a new system on live theatre records from home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who collects the children if you interview?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen could do Thursday pickup only if his grounds shift ends by three. I'd ask for the interview time and a written salary before treating a job as an escape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marsh & Finch staff that full AGI in 2028 can do our accounts and tax thinking work, so a staffing plan needs dates and names. I would also ask what clients can do when a machine gets a return wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My desk is exposed in 2028, not when hands-on robots appear around 2031. I expect the firm to cut some accountants and could lose my lower-paid role; Owen's outdoor work may also face robots later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd pause the children's paid swimming for a term and add the fifty monthly fee to our mortgage buffer. In the first year after 2028, if my post ends, I'd apply for posted salaried housing-association rent-accounts roles and ask for mortgage help if eligible, while Owen and I keep any paid hours we can get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. The mortgage and two children leave no room for a long unpaid search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about swimming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we will use the free pool sessions until the buffer holds a full mortgage payment. The children won't like it, but they should hear a real plan, not a vague promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you work evenings while you search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a paid evening box-office shift only if the theatre confirms the rate and Owen can cover the children. I would not budget money from a shift nobody has offered.

I would ask for a **client appeal route** after machine errors.
think: My **lower-paid desk role** could go when AGI arrives in 2028.
Owen’s **outdoor work** may face robots around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to see whether housing groups need people who can explain rent ledgers to families. I would want paid practice, not a course fee handed to a household with a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031 I'd still owe on the house, and AGI could prepare the theatre accounts I know. Owen's hands-on grounds work may face robots around 2034, so I cannot plan as if his wage is permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the housing association for a paid work-shadow day next year only if Marsh & Finch keeps my salary and the association has a supervisor. In the first year after 2031, if my firm cuts my paid days, I'd apply for posted salaried rent-accounts jobs and keep current funded hours until a written wage and start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, although five years gives me time to test whether the work suits me. I cannot leave a wage for an interesting tour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for on that day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch how a rent clerk explains an arrears letter to a tenant and where each payment is recorded. I would take a paid shift doing it only after the supervisor lets me try with someone present.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the association has no paid place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Marsh & Finch and ask the staff group to press for another funded option. We would keep saving twenty-five weekly while both wages arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the firm ten years is time to build paid reporting work for arts groups that still need a person to explain grants. The staff should see the fees before anyone calls it a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, our children may be out of school, but the mortgage could still be there. AGI reaches the desk then; robots around 2039 may change Owen's grounds work later, so a decade of wages matters now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add eighty a month to mortgage principal while both of us work full hours and ask Marsh & Finch to pilot paid quarterly grant reports for four local theatres, with fees going to the firm. In the first year after 2036, if three theatres renew at a price covering my hours, I'd stay salaried; otherwise I'd apply for posted housing finance roles and keep any funded firm work until a written offer starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, because ten years could shrink the loan but cannot promise work at 53. I would want proof the theatres pay twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a report show a theatre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show how ticket sales, donations and grant spending fit together, in words volunteers can use. If the second report doesn't earn a fee, we stop treating it as a job plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early if the mortgage shrinks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, less than a month saved today is nowhere near that. I'd rather work while we can and take the debt down slowly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a lost accountancy wage could break the mortgage before we save one full payment. Paid supervised practice in rent accounts, a posted salary and a real childcare plan would help. A fast tool cannot pick up my children when both adults are working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whose wages pay for the hour spent explaining a wrong automated rent letter. A family should never have to guess whether a machine or a person can correct a bill.

headlineQuote: A fast tool cannot pick up my children when both adults are working.
portrait: Freya, **43**, is an experienced, average-skilled accountant at Marsh & Finch with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification.
Her **low pay**, under-one-month buffer and few nearby firms leave a mortgage exposed to lost hours.
She uses AI **daily** on theatre ticket records, while Owen’s weather-dependent grounds shifts support two school-age children.
She fears **2028 job cuts** most and seeks funded rent-accounts practice or a paid firm grant-report service.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her wage before the household saves one mortgage payment.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid supervised practice**, a posted salary and workable childcare would help her move.
